newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Rep Leach still opposed to commerce-bank mix.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Rep Leach still opposed to commerce-bank mix.

text.p: House Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach said Wednesday he remained opposed to legislation allowing banks to combine with commercial firms, but also continued to indicate he was open to a carefully crafted, more modest approach.

Leach, along with most in congress and the industry, agreed that banks should be allowed to combine with other financial services firms. But the Iowa Republican outlined his opposition to several legislative proposals that would go further and allow banks to combine with non-financial firms.

"I'm committed to advancing an agenda that modernizes the financial services industry, but one that does not significantly break down the commerce and banking barrier or undercut the Fed," he said in the prepared text of a speech to the American Bankers Association Legislative Liason Advisory Committee here. "Bank modernization is achievable if people don't over-reach."
Leach gave some ground in the speech, suggesting an approach allowing a minimum of mixing, with limited non-financial activity based on a percentage of a bank's total capital.
Leach again blasted an approach contained in a bill introduced by Rep Richard Baker, Republican of Alabama, that would allow unlimited combinations.

"In my view, this is the most important 'don't,'" Leach said. "In barest terms, such a step would open the doors to a vast restructuring of America's business place and abandonment of the the traditional role of banking as an impartial provider of credit."
Leach also rejected a possible compromise bill introduced by Rep Marge Roukema, Republican on New Jersey, and Rep Bruce Vento, Democrat of Minnesota.
That bill, backed by an alliance of financial service trade groups, would allow a bank to do up to 25 percent of its business, referred to as a limited "basket," in non-financial activities.

Leach said a limit based on business activity was too broad and would lead to excessive concentration. "It is clear that big basket approaches will lead quickly to mega mergers and that the most vulnerable parties remain banks," he said. "The business activity definition is a chutzpah-laden paradigm shift containing a number of perplexing ramifications," he added.
As an alternative, Leach reiterated language he used in recent congressional testimony. A basket based on a percentage of capital would allow far less mixing of banks and commercial firms, he said.

"If it seems that modest investment experimentation should be granted banks, a basket that related to capital rather than business activity might, at least initially, be more prudential and less market distorting," Leach said.

Leach also repeated his support for assigning a major regulatory role to the Federal Reserve in any bank reform legislation. "For the Fed to provide services prudently at and coordinate effectively with central banks abroad, it would seem folly to cut its cord to the financial community," he said.
